raw_text:
The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) reduces sudden cardiac death in selected survivors of ventricular arrhythmia and in high-risk primary-prevention populations [1-3]. Conventional transvenous ICDs, however, expose patients to intravascular lead failure, venous occlusion, endocarditis, and extraction risk, problems that become especially important in young patients and those requiring decades of therapy [4,5]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to preserve defibrillator protection while avoiding transvenous and intracardiac hardware [6].

The S-ICD consists of a laterally placed pulse generator and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode. It senses a far-field subcutaneous electrocardiogram and delivers high-energy shocks for ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, but it cannot provide chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP). Early clinical studies established the feasibility of entirely extrathoracic defibrillation, with successful induced ventricular fibrillation conversion and acceptable short-term safety [6-8]. Experience subsequently expanded to patients with congenital heart disease and younger patients, in whom avoiding venous access and lead extraction is particularly attractive [9,10].

Patient selection is central. The ideal candidate has an ICD indication but no need for permanent pacing, resynchronization, or ATP for recurrent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Pre-implant electrocardiographic screening is required because myopotential, low-amplitude QRS, and prominent T waves can cause oversensing; screening failure is more common in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, and abnormal repolarization patterns [14,15]. Procedural refinements, especially the two-incision and intermuscular generator approaches, have simplified implantation and improved cosmetic and comfort outcomes [11]. Defibrillation testing has historically been performed because of the extrathoracic shock vector, although contemporary practice increasingly individualizes testing based on patient risk and implant position.

The dominant early limitation of S-ICD therapy was inappropriate shock, usually from T-wave oversensing rather than supraventricular tachycardia. The START study showed that S-ICD discrimination could compare favorably with transvenous ICD algorithms under controlled conditions [12]. Clinical registries nevertheless demonstrated that sensing quality, vector selection, and programming are critical [13]. Newer sensing filters and algorithms, including morphology-based discrimination and SMART Pass filtering, have substantially reduced inappropriate therapy [23,24]. Programming with higher conditional and shock zones, modeled partly on lessons from transvenous ICD programming, is now standard when clinically appropriate.

Large prospective studies support the effectiveness of the S-ICD. The US investigational device exemption study demonstrated high defibrillation efficacy and acceptable complication rates [16]. EFFORTLESS and pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS analyses confirmed durable shock efficacy, with complications dominated by infection, hematoma, discomfort, and lead or pocket issues rather than systemic bloodstream infection or endovascular lead failure [17,18]. Longer observational follow-up showed stable performance and low rates of late lead-related failure compared with historical transvenous experience [19,20]. The US post-approval study and UNTOUCHED trial further demonstrated favorable outcomes in contemporary primary-prevention patients with reduced ejection fraction, including lower inappropriate shock rates than in early experience [21,22].

Randomized evidence has clarified comparative effectiveness. The PRAETORIAN trial found the S-ICD noninferior to the transvenous ICD for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [25,26]. The pattern of events differed: transvenous systems retained advantages for ATP and pacing, whereas S-ICD systems avoided lead-related endovascular complications. Implant positioning remains important; the PRAETORIAN score was proposed to identify radiographic features associated with ineffective conversion and to guide repositioning when needed [27]. Meta-analytic data generally align with trial evidence, suggesting similar mortality and appropriate shock efficacy but fewer lead-related complications and more residual inappropriate shocks in older S-ICD cohorts [30].

The S-ICD is particularly appealing after extraction for infection or lead malfunction, in dialysis patients with limited venous access and high infection risk, and in inherited arrhythmia syndromes where pacing is rarely required [28,29]. Its main disadvantages remain absence of ATP and pacing, larger generator size, potential discomfort, and the need for screening and careful sensing management. Future development is likely to focus on smaller devices, longer battery life, improved discrimination, communication with leadless pacemakers, and more precise risk stratification for ATP need. In current practice, the S-ICD is best viewed not as a universal replacement for the transvenous ICD, but as a mature alternative for appropriately selected patients in whom the long-term hazards of transvenous leads outweigh the benefits of pacing capability.
